# cpal - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cpal/0.17.3/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/cpal/index.html

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#how-to-use-cpal)How to use cpal

Here are some concepts cpal exposes:

- A `Host`[default_host](https://docs.rs/platform/fn.default_host.html)that is guaranteed to be available.
- A `Device`
- A `Stream`[Device](https://docs.rs/platform/struct.Device.html)will run your stream before you can create one. Often, a default device can be retrieved via the[Host](https://docs.rs/platform/struct.Host.html).

The first step is to initialise the [ Host](https://docs.rs/platform/struct.Host.html):

```
use cpal::traits::HostTrait;
let host = cpal::default_host();
```
Then choose an available [ Device](https://docs.rs/platform/struct.Device.html). The easiest way is to use the default input or output

`Device` via the [or](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.HostTrait.html#tymethod.default_input_device)

`default_input_device()`[methods on](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.HostTrait.html#tymethod.default_output_device)

`default_output_device()``host`.Alternatively, you can enumerate all the available devices with the [ devices()](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.HostTrait.html#tymethod.devices) method.
Beware that the

`default_*_device()` functions return an `Option<Device>` in case no device
is available for that stream type on the system.`let device = host.default_output_device().expect("no output device available");`Before we can create a stream, we must decide what the configuration of the audio stream is
going to be.
You can query all the supported configurations with the
[ supported_input_configs()](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.DeviceTrait.html#tymethod.supported_input_configs) and

[methods. These produce a list of](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.DeviceTrait.html#tymethod.supported_output_configs)

`supported_output_configs()`[structs which can later be turned into actual](https://docs.rs/struct.SupportedStreamConfigRange.html)

`SupportedStreamConfigRange`[structs.](https://docs.rs/struct.SupportedStreamConfig.html)

`SupportedStreamConfig`If you don’t want to query the list of configs,
you can also build your own [ StreamConfig](https://docs.rs/struct.StreamConfig.html) manually, but doing so could lead to an error when
building the stream if the config is not supported by the device.

Note: the`supported_input/output_configs()`methods could return an error for example if the device has been disconnected.

```
use cpal::traits::{DeviceTrait, HostTrait};
let mut supported_configs_range = device.supported_output_configs()
    .expect("error while querying configs");
let supported_config = supported_configs_range.next()
    .expect("no supported config?!")
    .with_max_sample_rate();
```
Now that we have everything for the stream, we are ready to create it from our selected device:

```
use cpal::Data;
use cpal::traits::{DeviceTrait, HostTrait, StreamTrait};
let stream = device.build_output_stream(
    &config,
    move |data: &mut [f32], _: &cpal::OutputCallbackInfo| {
        // react to stream events and read or write stream data here.
    },
    move |err| {
        // react to errors here.
    },
    None // None=blocking, Some(Duration)=timeout
);
```
While the stream is running, the selected audio device will periodically call the data callback
that was passed to the function. For input streams, the callback receives `&`[ Data](https://docs.rs/struct.Data.html) containing
captured audio samples. For output streams, the callback receives

`&mut`[to be filled with audio samples for playback.](https://docs.rs/struct.Data.html)

`Data`

Note: Creating and running a stream willnotblock the thread. On modern platforms, the given callback is called by a dedicated, high-priority thread responsible for delivering audio data to the system’s audio device in a timely manner. On older platforms that only provide a blocking API (e.g. ALSA), CPAL will create a thread in order to consistently provide non-blocking behaviour (currently this is a thread per stream, but this may change to use a single thread for all streams).If this is an issue for your platform or design, please share your issue and use-case with the CPAL team on the GitHub issue tracker for consideration.

In this example, we simply fill the given output buffer with silence.

```
use cpal::{Data, Sample, SampleFormat, FromSample};
use cpal::traits::{DeviceTrait, HostTrait, StreamTrait};
let err_fn = |err| eprintln!("an error occurred on the output audio stream: {}", err);
let sample_format = supported_config.sample_format();
let config = supported_config.into();
let stream = match sample_format {
    SampleFormat::F32 => device.build_output_stream(&config, write_silence::<f32>, err_fn, None),
    SampleFormat::I16 => device.build_output_stream(&config, write_silence::<i16>, err_fn, None),
    SampleFormat::U16 => device.build_output_stream(&config, write_silence::<u16>, err_fn, None),
    sample_format => panic!("Unsupported sample format '{sample_format}'")
}.unwrap();
fn write_silence<T: Sample>(data: &mut [T], _: &cpal::OutputCallbackInfo) {
    for sample in data.iter_mut() {
        *sample = Sample::EQUILIBRIUM;
    }
}
```
Not all platforms automatically run the stream upon creation. To ensure the stream has started,
we can use [ Stream::play](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.StreamTrait.html#tymethod.play).

`stream.play().unwrap();`Some devices support pausing the audio stream. This can be useful for saving energy in moments of silence.

`stream.pause().unwrap();`## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Backend](https://docs.rs/struct.BackendSpecificError.html)- Specific - Error
- Some error has occurred that is specific to the backend from which it was produced.
- [Data](https://docs.rs/struct.Data.html)
- A buffer of dynamically typed audio data, passed to raw stream callbacks.
- [Device](https://docs.rs/struct.DeviceId.html)- Id
- A stable identifier for an audio device across all supported platforms.
- [Host](https://docs.rs/struct.HostUnavailable.html)- Unavailable
- The requested host, although supported on this platform, is unavailable.
- [I24](https://docs.rs/struct.I24.html)
- 24-bit signed integer sample type.
- [Input](https://docs.rs/struct.InputCallbackInfo.html)- Callback - Info
- Information relevant to a single call to the user’s input stream data callback.
- [Input](https://docs.rs/struct.InputStreamTimestamp.html)- Stream - Timestamp
- A timestamp associated with a call to an input stream’s data callback.
- [Output](https://docs.rs/struct.OutputCallbackInfo.html)- Callback - Info
- Information relevant to a single call to the user’s output stream data callback.
- [Output](https://docs.rs/struct.OutputStreamTimestamp.html)- Stream - Timestamp
- A timestamp associated with a call to an output stream’s data callback.
- [Stream](https://docs.rs/struct.StreamConfig.html)- Config
- The set of parameters used to describe how to open a stream.
- [Stream](https://docs.rs/struct.StreamInstant.html)- Instant
- A monotonic time instance associated with a stream, retrieved from either:
- [Supported](https://docs.rs/struct.SupportedStreamConfig.html)- Stream - Config
- Describes a single supported stream configuration, retrieved via either a
`SupportedStreamConfigRange``Device::default_input/output_config`
- [Supported](https://docs.rs/struct.SupportedStreamConfigRange.html)- Stream - Config - Range
- Describes a range of supported stream configurations, retrieved via the
`Device::supported_input/output_configs`
- [U24](https://docs.rs/struct.U24.html)
- 24-bit unsigned integer sample type.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Buffer](https://docs.rs/enum.BufferSize.html)- Size
- The buffer size requests the callback size for audio streams.
- [Build](https://docs.rs/enum.BuildStreamError.html)- Stream - Error
- Error that can happen when creating a `Stream`
- [Default](https://docs.rs/enum.DefaultStreamConfigError.html)- Stream - Config - Error
- May occur when attempting to request the default input or output stream format from a `Device`
- [Device](https://docs.rs/enum.DeviceIdError.html)- IdError
- An error that may occur while attempting to retrieve a device ID.
- [Device](https://docs.rs/enum.DeviceNameError.html)- Name - Error
- An error that may occur while attempting to retrieve a device name.
- [Devices](https://docs.rs/enum.DevicesError.html)- Error
- An error that might occur while attempting to enumerate the available devices on a system.
- [Pause](https://docs.rs/enum.PauseStreamError.html)- Stream - Error
- Errors that might occur when calling `Stream::pause()`
- [Play](https://docs.rs/enum.PlayStreamError.html)- Stream - Error
- Errors that might occur when calling `Stream::play()`
- [Sample](https://docs.rs/enum.SampleFormat.html)- Format
- Format that each sample has. Usually, this corresponds to the sampling
depth of the audio source. For example, 16 bit quantized samples can be
encoded in `i16`or`u16`. Note that the quantized sampling depth is not directly visible for formats where`is_float`
- [Stream](https://docs.rs/enum.StreamError.html)- Error
- Errors that might occur while a stream is running.
- [Supported](https://docs.rs/enum.SupportedBufferSize.html)- Buffer - Size
- Describes the minimum and maximum supported buffer size for the device
- [Supported](https://docs.rs/enum.SupportedStreamConfigsError.html)- Stream - Configs - Error
- Error that can happen when enumerating the list of supported formats.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Channel](https://docs.rs/type.ChannelCount.html)- Count
- Number of channels.

- Iterator of devices wrapped in a filter to only include certain device types
- [Frame](https://docs.rs/type.FrameCount.html)- Count
- A frame represents one sample for each channel. For example, with stereo audio, one frame contains two samples (left and right channels).
- [Input](https://docs.rs/type.InputDevices.html)- Devices
- A host’s device iterator yielding only *input*devices.

- A host’s device iterator yielding only *output*devices.
- [Sample](https://docs.rs/type.SampleRate.html)- Rate
- The number of samples processed per second for a single channel of audio.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/cpal/lib.rs.html#858-922)#### pub fn [cmp_default_heuristics](https://docs.rs#method.cmp_default_heuristics)(&self, other: &Self) -> [Ordering](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/enum.Ordering.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/cpal/lib.rs.html#858-922)

#### pub fn [cmp_default_heuristics](https://docs.rs#method.cmp_default_heuristics)(&self, other: &Self) -> [Ordering](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/enum.Ordering.html)

A comparison function which compares two [ SupportedStreamConfigRange](https://docs.rs/struct.SupportedStreamConfigRange.html)s in terms of their priority of
use as a default stream format.

Some backends do not provide a default stream format for their audio devices. In these cases, CPAL attempts to decide on a reasonable default format for the user. To do this we use the “greatest” of all supported stream formats when compared with this method.

SupportedStreamConfigs are prioritised by the following heuristics:

**Channels**:

- Stereo
- Mono
- Max available channels

**Sample format**:

- f32
- i16
- u16

**Sample rate**:

- 44100 (cd quality)
- Max sample rate

# dasp_sample - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/dasp_sample/0.11.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/dasp_sample/index.html

## Expand description

Use the [ Sample](https://docs.rs/trait.Sample.html) trait to remain generic over sample types, easily
access sample type conversions, apply basic audio operations and more.

The **Sample** trait is the core abstraction throughout dasp on which most other abstractions
are based.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use conv::`- [Duplex](https://docs.rs/conv/trait.Duplex.html);
- `pub use conv::`- [FromSample](https://docs.rs/conv/trait.FromSample.html);
- `pub use conv::`- [ToSample](https://docs.rs/conv/trait.ToSample.html);
- `pub use types::`- [I24](https://docs.rs/types/i24/struct.I24.html);
- `pub use types::`- [I48](https://docs.rs/types/i48/struct.I48.html);
- `pub use types::`- [U24](https://docs.rs/types/u24/struct.U24.html);
- `pub use types::`- [U48](https://docs.rs/types/u48/struct.U48.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [conv](https://docs.rs/conv/index.html)
- Pure functions and traits for converting between i8, i16, I24, i32, I48, i64, u8, u16, U24, u32, U48, u64, f32 and f64.
- [types](https://docs.rs/types/index.html)
- A collection of custom, non-std **Sample**types.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Float](https://docs.rs/trait.FloatSample.html)- Sample
- Sample format types represented as floating point numbers.
- [Sample](https://docs.rs/trait.Sample.html)
- A trait for working generically across different **Sample**format types.
- [Signed](https://docs.rs/trait.SignedSample.html)- Sample
- Integral and floating-point **Sample**format types whose equilibrium is at 0.

# hrdr_editor - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/hrdr-editor/0.2.1/hrdr_editor/

## Expand description

`hrdr-editor` — the FSM-agnostic editing seam.

The rest of hrdr talks only to the [ EditorEngine](https://docs.rs/trait.EditorEngine.html) trait — never to vim
types. The concrete

[wraps the hjkl engine and drives it through](https://docs.rs/struct.VimEngine.html)

`VimEngine``hjkl_vim::dispatch_input`. When hjkl’s pluggable-FSM work (epic
#265) lands a vscode/helix discipline, add a sibling `EditorEngine` impl
and the TUI swaps it in with zero churn — it reads `mode_label()` /
`is_insert()` (projected from hjkl’s FSM-agnostic `CoarseMode`), not
`VimMode`.## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Editor](https://docs.rs/struct.EditorKey.html)- Key
- The seam’s renderer-agnostic key DTO — hjkl’s own toolkit-neutral
`Input { key, ctrl, alt, shift }`, re-exported so consumers never touch hjkl types directly. A key press with modifier flags. The vim engine reads modifiers directly off this struct (e.g.`input.ctrl && input.key == Key::Char('d')`).
- [Hrdr](https://docs.rs/struct.HrdrHost.html)- Host
- [Plain](https://docs.rs/struct.PlainEngine.html)- Engine
- A plain UTF-8 text buffer with a char-index cursor.
- [VimEngine](https://docs.rs/struct.VimEngine.html)
- The default discipline: hjkl’s vim FSM.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Editor](https://docs.rs/enum.EditorKeyCode.html)- KeyCode
- The seam’s renderer-agnostic key DTO — hjkl’s own toolkit-neutral
`Input { key, ctrl, alt, shift }`, re-exported so consumers never touch hjkl types directly. A key code, mirroring the subset of [`crossterm::event::KeyCode`] the vim engine actually consumes.`Null`is the conventional sentinel for “no input” (matching the previous`tui_textarea::Key`shape) so call sites can early-return on unsupported keys.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Editor](https://docs.rs/trait.EditorEngine.html)- Engine
- A pluggable editing discipline — the renderer-agnostic core of the seam.
- [TuiEditor](https://docs.rs/trait.TuiEditorEngine.html)- Engine
- What the TUI hosts: both halves of the seam.
- [TuiRender](https://docs.rs/trait.TuiRender.html)
- The terminal renderer half of the seam (ratatui). Kept out of
`EditorEngine`

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [key_](https://docs.rs/fn.key_from_crossterm.html)- from_ - crossterm
- Convert a crossterm key event to the seam’s `EditorKey``None`for key-release events, which must not reach the engines (terminals reporting them would double keystrokes).

# hrdr_agent - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/hrdr-agent/0.2.1/hrdr_agent/

## Expand description

`hrdr-agent` — the agentic loop.

Drives an OpenAI-compatible model through tool calls until a coding task is
complete: stream a turn, execute any requested tools, feed the results back,
repeat. Emits [ AgentEvent](https://docs.rs/enum.AgentEvent.html)s for a UI (or stdout) to render live.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Agent](https://docs.rs/struct.Agent.html)
- A running agent: model client + tools + conversation state.
- [Agent](https://docs.rs/struct.AgentConfig.html)- Config
- Agent configuration.
- [Checkpoint](https://docs.rs/struct.CheckpointInfo.html)- Info
- One revertible checkpoint (a turn that changed files).
- [File](https://docs.rs/struct.FileCheckpoints.html)- Checkpoints
- A disk-backed store of per-turn file pre-images.
- [Guardrail](https://docs.rs/struct.GuardrailConfig.html)- Config
- One user-defined shell guardrail from a `[[guardrails]]`config entry: commands matching`pattern`(a regex) are rejected with`message`. Applied on top of the built-in rules (`hrdr_tools::default_guardrails`).
- [Hook](https://docs.rs/struct.HookConfig.html)- Config
- One post-edit hook from a `[[hooks]]`config entry: after tool`on`(`edit`,`write_file`, or`*`) successfully mutates a file matching`glob`, run shell command`run`(`{path}`is substituted). Formatters, mostly. Failures surface as warnings in the tool result, never as errors.
- [Message](https://docs.rs/struct.Message.html)
- A single chat message. Used for both request and response — `content`is optional because assistant turns that only call tools carry no text.
- [Provider](https://docs.rs/struct.ProviderConfig.html)- Config
- A user-defined provider from `[providers.<name>]`in config.
- [Resolved](https://docs.rs/struct.ResolvedProvider.html)- Provider
- A fully-resolved provider preset.
- [Session](https://docs.rs/struct.Session.html)
- A saved conversation.
- [Session](https://docs.rs/struct.SessionMeta.html)- Meta
- Lightweight directory listing entry.
- [Todo](https://docs.rs/struct.Todo.html)
- A single TODO item tracked by `todo_write`.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Agent](https://docs.rs/enum.AgentEvent.html)- Event
- Events emitted as a turn progresses.
- [Config](https://docs.rs/enum.ConfigValue.html)- Value
- A value to persist into the user config file.
- [Message](https://docs.rs/enum.MessageRole.html)- Role
- Message author role.

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [DEFAULT_](https://docs.rs/constant.DEFAULT_AUTO_COMPACT.html)- AUTO_ - COMPACT
- Default auto-compaction trigger: 85% of the context window (leaves headroom so the next turn doesn’t overflow).

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [builtin_](https://docs.rs/fn.builtin_provider.html)- provider
- Resolve a built-in provider name (case-insensitive).
- [config_](https://docs.rs/fn.config_dir.html)- dir
- `hrdr`’s config directory —- `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/hrdr`, default- `~/.config/hrdr`(cross-platform via home-dir detection). Shared by- `config.toml`loading and the global- `AGENTS.md`lookup so the two can’t diverge.
- [config_](https://docs.rs/fn.config_file_path.html)- file_ - path
- Path to the user config file (`~/.config/hrdr/config.toml`), if`HOME`is set.
- [cwd_](https://docs.rs/fn.cwd_slug.html)- slug
- Slug for a working directory — the per-cwd subdirectory name. The full path
is flattened (e.g. `/home/me/Projects/foo`→`home-me-projects-foo`).
- [gather_](https://docs.rs/fn.gather_agent_docs.html)- agent_ - docs
- Collect project instructions from `AGENTS.md`files, walking from`cwd`up to the filesystem root, plus an optional global`~/.config/hrdr/AGENTS.md`. Less specific files (global, then ancestors) come first so nearer files override by appearing later. Returns`None`if nothing is found.
- [in_](https://docs.rs/fn.in_git_repo.html)- git_ - repo
- Whether `cwd`(or an ancestor) is inside a git repo.`.git`may be a directory (normal) or a file (worktrees/submodules).
- [list_](https://docs.rs/fn.list_sessions.html)- sessions
- List saved sessions across every working directory, newest first. Also
picks up legacy flat-layout files written directly under `sessions/`.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_env_bool.html)- env_ - bool
- Parse a boolean-ish env value; `None`(leave the current value) if it’s not one of the recognized on/off spellings. Parse a boolean setting from a config/CLI/env string, accepting the common spellings (`1`/`0`,`true`/`false`,`on`/`off`,`yes`/`no`, case-insensitive). Returns`None`for anything unrecognized so callers can leave the current value unchanged.
- [persist_](https://docs.rs/fn.persist_setting.html)- setting
- Set `key = value`in the user config file (creating it if needed), preserving existing keys, ordering, and comments. Returns the file path.
- [remove_](https://docs.rs/fn.remove_setting.html)- setting
- Remove `key`from the user config file (if present). Returns the file path.
- [render_](https://docs.rs/fn.render_system.html)- system
- Render the agent system prompt for the given tool set and working directory.
`instructions`is the gathered AGENTS.md content (see`gather_agent_docs`
- [resolve_](https://docs.rs/fn.resolve_session.html)- session
- Resolve a `/resume`argument to`(id, Session)`. Looks in`cwd`’s directory first (by file id), then scans every directory — preferring the current`cwd`— matching the file id or the display`name`(case-insensitive, e.g. after`/rename`).
- [session_](https://docs.rs/fn.session_dir.html)- dir
- The per-cwd directory a session lives in.
- [sessions_](https://docs.rs/fn.sessions_dir.html)- dir
- `$XDG_DATA_HOME/hrdr/sessions`, or- `~/.local/share/hrdr/sessions`.
- [unique_](https://docs.rs/fn.unique_session_id.html)- session_ - id
- A collision-free file id (within `cwd`’s directory) derived from`name`: the slug, then`slug-2`,`slug-3`, … if files already exist.

# sandogasa_meetbot - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sandogasa-meetbot/0.15.3/sandogasa_meetbot/

## Expand description

HTTP client for [meetbot.fedoraproject.org](https://meetbot.fedoraproject.org/)’s
meeting search endpoint.

Meetbot exposes a single lightweight JSON endpoint for the “Search for conversations” UI in its web frontend. This crate wraps that endpoint behind a typed client.

```
use sandogasa_meetbot::Meetbot;
let client = Meetbot::new();
for meeting in client.search("centos-hyperscale-sig")? {
    println!("{} {}", meeting.datetime, meeting.summary_url);
}
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [DEFAULT_](https://docs.rs/constant.DEFAULT_BASE_URL.html)- BASE_ - URL
- Default production base URL for meetbot’s web frontend.
- [PUBLIC_](https://docs.rs/constant.PUBLIC_ARTEFACT_BASE.html)- ARTEFACT_ - BASE
- Default base URL used for public meeting artefacts (log /
summary HTML). Distinct from the web frontend: the JSON
endpoint returns URLs on `meetbot-raw.fedoraproject.org`, but users typically want to link to the public-facing`meetbot.fedoraproject.org`host instead.`Meetbot::search`applies this rewrite.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [dedup_](https://docs.rs/fn.dedup_by_longest_log.html)- by_ - longest_ - log
- Collapse same-day duplicates in a meeting list by keeping
the entry whose `logs_url`is the largest, as a rough proxy for “the meeting that actually happened” when`!startmeeting`was run multiple times (on the same channel, or across overlapping channels) on a single day.`on_warning`is invoked once per collapsed group with`(winner, dropped)`so the caller can surface it to the user.

# camel_language_rhai - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/camel-language-rhai/0.22.0/camel_language_rhai/

## Expand description

camel-language-rhai — Rhai script language for Camel Rust.

Main types: `RhaiLanguage`, `RhaiExpression`, `RhaiPredicate`, `RhaiMutatingExpression`.
Scripts have access to `body`, `headers`, `header()`, `set_header()`, `property()`, `set_property()`.

[§](https://docs.rs#resource-limits)Resource Limits

Scripts are bounded by configurable limits sourced from `[languages.rhai.limits]`
in `Camel.toml`. When absent, the rust-camel runtime defaults apply:

| Limit | Default |
|---|---|
| `max-operations` | 100,000 |
| `max-string-size` | 1 MiB |
| `max-array-size` | 10,000 elements |
| `max-map-size` | 10,000 entries |
| `max-expression-depth` | 64 |
| `max-function-expression-depth` | 32 |
| `execution-timeout-ms` | 5,000 |

Every limit is `Option<_>`; `None` means “use rust-camel runtime default” (no
default-lie per ADR-0011).

[§](https://docs.rs#covered-threats)Covered threats

- Infinite loops (`loop {}`) — trip`max-operations`and`execution-timeout-ms`(whichever fires first).
- Oversized allocations — strings, arrays, maps each have size caps.
- Pathological nesting — expression and function-expression depths are bounded.

[§](https://docs.rs#timeout-caveat)Timeout caveat

`execution-timeout-ms` wraps `eval_with_scope` in `tokio::time::timeout` +
`spawn_blocking`. When the timeout fires, the route future resolves to an
error, but the blocking thread may continue executing until the script
trips `max-operations` or finishes. This is the same partial-mitigation
caveat shared with the Boa engine.

[§](https://docs.rs#sandboxing)Sandboxing

Rhai scripts **cannot access the host filesystem, network APIs, or Rhai
module loading**. This sandbox is **unconditional** — there is no config
opt-out.

Two structural layers enforce this:

- **Compile time**— the Rhai- `no_module`cargo feature (see root- `Cargo.toml`) disables module loading across the entire crate graph.
- **Runtime**— engines are built via- `Engine::new_raw()`plus an explicit- `StandardPackage`registration. Unlike- `Engine::new()`, this does not install a- `FileModuleResolver`.

Additionally, `eval` and `import` are registered as disabled symbols as
defense in depth (no-op safe if symbols are absent). If a future Rhai
package were to re-introduce module loading or dynamic evaluation, these
symbols would still be blocked to user scripts.

What the sandbox is **not**:

- It is not a CPU/memory cap. Those are separate resource limits; see rc-bpx.
- It does not block timing APIs (`sleep`,`timestamp`). Those remain part of`StandardPackage`; CPU/time-based DoS is covered by rc-bpx resource limits.
- It is not a side-channel defense (cache timing, memory layout). Out of scope.

If your integration genuinely needs filesystem or network access from a
route script, use the explicit Camel components (`file:`, `http:`) with
their own runtime policies — do not attempt to bypass this sandbox.

[§](https://docs.rs#limitations)Limitations

- Resource limits (max operations, string/array/map sizes, expression
depths) are enforced as denial-of-service protection, not as a sandbox.
They are configurable — see [# Resource Limits](https://docs.rs#resource-limits)above.
- The `body`variable is always a string. Structured access to JSON/XML bodies requires explicit parsing within the script using Rhai’s built-in map/array types.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Rhai](https://docs.rs/struct.RhaiLanguage.html)- Language
- Rhai scripting language for rust-camel.

# sandogasa_koji - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sandogasa-koji/0.15.3/sandogasa_koji/

## Expand description

Koji build system CLI wrapper.

Provides functions for querying Koji tags and builds by shelling
out to the `koji` CLI. Supports multiple Koji profiles (e.g.
`cbs` for CentOS Build System).

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [TagAdd](https://docs.rs/struct.TagAddEvent.html)- Event
- One “tagged into” event from `koji list-history --tag=<tag>`. Captures only the bits the activity-reporting code needs; the date column is parsed by the caller as needed.
- [Tagged](https://docs.rs/struct.TaggedBuild.html)- Build
- A build found in a Koji tag.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [build_](https://docs.rs/fn.build_creation_date.html)- creation_ - date
- Parse the build’s creation date from `koji buildinfo`.
- [build_](https://docs.rs/fn.build_info_with_changelog.html)- info_ - with_ - changelog
- Fetch `koji buildinfo --changelog <nvr>`output verbatim for display. Returns the raw stdout so callers can show it to a human reviewing the build. Errors propagate (unlike the date/rpm helpers, an unexpected failure here is worth surfacing during an interactive review).
- [build_](https://docs.rs/fn.build_rpms.html)- rpms
- List binary RPM names for a build via `koji buildinfo`.
- [check_](https://docs.rs/fn.check_auth.html)- auth
- Verify an authenticated Koji session is available for `profile`by running`koji moshimoshi`(the authenticated hello).
- [list_](https://docs.rs/fn.list_tagged.html)- tagged
- List builds in a Koji tag with their owners.
- [list_](https://docs.rs/fn.list_tagged_nvrs.html)- tagged_ - nvrs
- List NVRs in a Koji tag (quiet mode, NVRs only).
- [list_](https://docs.rs/fn.list_tagged_package_names.html)- tagged_ - package_ - names
- List the latest source package names tagged into a Koji tag.
- [list_](https://docs.rs/fn.list_tags.html)- tags
- List Koji tag names matching a glob `pattern`(e.g.`hyperscale10s-*-release`). Wraps`koji list-tags <pattern>`.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_nvr.html)- nvr
- Parse an NVR string into (name, version, release).
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_nvr_name.html)- nvr_ - name
- Parse an NVR string into the package name.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_tag_history.html)- tag_ - history
- Parse `koji list-history`output and pick out only the “tagged into” entries. Format of those lines (as of koji 1.34,`--utc`):
- [regen_](https://docs.rs/fn.regen_repo.html)- repo
- Regenerate a Koji tag’s repo (`koji regen-repo --wait <tag>`).
- [tag_](https://docs.rs/fn.tag_build.html)- build
- Tag a build into a Koji tag (`koji tag-build --wait <tag> <nvr>`).
- [tag_](https://docs.rs/fn.tag_history.html)- history
- Walk a tag’s “tagged into” events in the window `[after, before)`and return them in chronological order. Implemented via`koji list-history --tag=<tag>`parsed line-by-line; only`tagged into`lines are kept (other event types like owner changes and untags are filtered out).
- [untag_](https://docs.rs/fn.untag_build.html)- build
- Untag a build from a Koji tag (`koji untag-build <tag> <nvr>`).

# hrdr_tools - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/hrdr-tools/0.2.1/hrdr_tools/

## Expand description

`hrdr-tools` — the agentic tool set.

The locked MVP set: `read_file`, `write_file`, `edit`, `bash`, `grep`,
`glob`, `todo_write`. Each implements [ Tool](https://docs.rs/trait.Tool.html) and is exposed to the model
as a native OpenAI function. Efficiency is in the design: token-bounded
outputs, line-numbered reads for precise edits, ripgrep-backed search.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Bash](https://docs.rs/struct.BashTool.html)- Tool
- [Checkpoint](https://docs.rs/struct.CheckpointInfo.html)- Info
- One revertible checkpoint (a turn that changed files).
- [Checkpoints](https://docs.rs/struct.Checkpoints.html)
- A disk-backed store of per-turn file pre-images.
- [Edit](https://docs.rs/struct.EditTool.html)- Tool
- [Glob](https://docs.rs/struct.GlobTool.html)- Tool
- [Grep](https://docs.rs/struct.GrepTool.html)- Tool
- [Guardrail](https://docs.rs/struct.Guardrail.html)
- One command rule: a regex matched against the whole shell command line and the corrective message returned to the model when it matches.
- [Hook](https://docs.rs/struct.Hook.html)
- One configured hook: run `run`(with`{path}`substituted) after tool`on`successfully mutates a file matching`glob`.
- [Power](https://docs.rs/struct.PowerShellTool.html)- Shell - Tool
- [Read](https://docs.rs/struct.ReadTool.html)- Tool
- [Todo](https://docs.rs/struct.TodoItem.html)- Item
- A single TODO item tracked by `todo_write`.
- [Todo](https://docs.rs/struct.TodoTool.html)- Tool
- [Tool](https://docs.rs/struct.ToolContext.html)- Context
- Shared execution context handed to every tool call.
- [Tool](https://docs.rs/struct.ToolRegistry.html)- Registry
- Ordered registry of tools, keyed by name.
- [WebFetch](https://docs.rs/struct.WebFetchTool.html)- Tool
- [WebSearch](https://docs.rs/struct.WebSearchTool.html)- Tool
- [Write](https://docs.rs/struct.WriteTool.html)- Tool

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [DEFAULT_](https://docs.rs/constant.DEFAULT_HOOK_TIMEOUT_MS.html)- HOOK_ - TIMEOUT_ - MS
- Default per-hook timeout: formatters are fast; anything slower is stuck.
- [DEFAULT_](https://docs.rs/constant.DEFAULT_MAX_OUTPUT.html)- MAX_ - OUTPUT
- Default cap on a single tool’s textual output, in bytes. Larger results are truncated with a marker so the model’s context is never blown by one call.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Tool](https://docs.rs/trait.Tool.html)
- A model-callable tool.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [available_](https://docs.rs/fn.available_shell_tools.html)- shell_ - tools
- The available shell tools for this machine (bash and/or PowerShell), only
including a tool when its interpreter is actually on `PATH`.
- [cap_](https://docs.rs/fn.cap_matches.html)- matches
- Cap search output at `max_matches`*matches*, appending a count of what was dropped and how to narrow the search. Only`path:NN:…`lines count as matches —`path-NN-…`context lines and`--`group separators (grep/rg`-C`format) ride along with their match, so a context-grep isn’t over-counted.
- [check_](https://docs.rs/fn.check_guardrails.html)- guardrails
- First matching rule’s message, if `command`trips any guardrail. Quoted spans are blanked before matching so string*arguments*that merely mention a blocked command (e.g.`rg 'git add -A'`) don’t false-positive.
- [default_](https://docs.rs/fn.default_guardrails.html)- guardrails
- The built-in rules. Patterns are matched anywhere in the command string
(compound `a && b`commands included). Kept deliberately narrow: they block the exact foot-gun spellings, not whole subcommands.
- [floor_](https://docs.rs/fn.floor_char_boundary.html)- char_ - boundary
- Largest byte index `≤ max`that lies on a UTF-8 char boundary of`s`, so`&s[..floor_char_boundary(s, max)]`never panics on multibyte text. Returns`s.len()`when`max >= s.len()`. (std’s`str::floor_char_boundary`is still unstable, hence this helper.)
- [run_](https://docs.rs/fn.run_file_hooks.html)- file_ - hooks
- Run every hook matching (`tool`,`path`) sequentially, returning one warning line per hook that failed or timed out (empty = all quiet). Success output is discarded — the caller re-reads the file and diffs, so the model sees the effect, not the chatter.
- [truncate](https://docs.rs/fn.truncate.html)
- Truncate `text`to`max`bytes on a char boundary, appending a marker that tells the model output was cut.
- [truncate_](https://docs.rs/fn.truncate_inline.html)- inline
- Collapse `s`to a single line (newlines → spaces) and truncate to`max`**characters**, appending`…`if it was cut. For compact one-line previews (tool-arg previews, status lines) — width-based, unlike the byte-based`truncate`
- [truncate_](https://docs.rs/fn.truncate_middle.html)- middle
- Truncate to `max`bytes keeping the**head and tail**with the omission in the middle. For shell output: build/test runs put the errors at the end, so head-only truncation (plain`truncate`
- [unix_](https://docs.rs/fn.unix_now.html)- now
- Current Unix time in whole seconds (0 if the clock is before the epoch). Shared by checkpoint journaling and session metadata.

# hrdr_llm - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/hrdr-llm/0.2.1/hrdr_llm/

## Expand description

`hrdr-llm` — a thin, provider-agnostic OpenAI chat-completions client.

Points at any `/v1/chat/completions` endpoint via `base_url` (OpenAI,
`infr`, llama.cpp, OpenRouter, …). Supports native tool calls and SSE
streaming with tool-call reassembly via [ Accumulator](https://docs.rs/struct.Accumulator.html).

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- Folds streaming chunks back into a single assistant `ChatMessage`
- [Chat](https://docs.rs/struct.ChatChunk.html)- Chunk
- One `chat.completion.chunk`SSE event. The final chunk (when`include_usage`is set) carries`usage`with empty`choices`.
- [Chat](https://docs.rs/struct.ChatMessage.html)- Message
- A single chat message. Used for both request and response — `content`is optional because assistant turns that only call tools carry no text.
- [Chat](https://docs.rs/struct.ChatRequest.html)- Request
- Request body for `POST /v1/chat/completions`.
- [Chunk](https://docs.rs/struct.ChunkChoice.html)- Choice
- [Client](https://docs.rs/struct.Client.html)
- A configured chat-completions client.

- [Function](https://docs.rs/struct.FunctionDef.html)- Def
- [Tool](https://docs.rs/struct.ToolCall.html)- Call

- A tool definition advertised to the model in the request `tools[]`.
- [Usage](https://docs.rs/struct.Usage.html)

GitLab REST and GraphQL API client for issues and work items.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- Client for the GitLab REST API v4.

- One entry from the user-activity events endpoint. Fields are
sparse — GitLab only populates the ones relevant to each
`action_name`.

- A GitLab user as returned by `/users?username=<name>`.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [count_](https://docs.rs/fn.count_authored_commits.html)- authored_ - commits
- Count commits in `project_id`authored by`author`within`[since, until]`(inclusive). GitLab’s commits endpoint matches the`author`parameter against both name and email fields, so passing the GitLab username usually works; if the user authored commits under an email only, pass that email string instead.
- [list_](https://docs.rs/fn.list_archived_project_names.html)- archived_ - project_ - names
- List the **archived**projects under a GitLab group, returning their names. GitLab’s`archived=true`filter narrows the listing server-side, so this is a cheap separate query rather than enriching every project in the main listing.
- [list_](https://docs.rs/fn.list_group_projects.html)- group_ - projects
- List all projects under a GitLab group (public, no auth needed).
- [list_](https://docs.rs/fn.list_tags.html)- tags
- List tags for a project, paginated. Returns an empty list on
404. Uses `order_by=updated&sort=desc`so newer tags come first — handy when the caller wants to short-circuit on the first tag older than its window of interest.
- [package_](https://docs.rs/fn.package_from_issue_url.html)- from_ - issue_ - url
- Extract the package name from a GitLab issue or work item web_url.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_issue_url.html)- issue_ - url
- Parse a GitLab issue / work-item URL into its components.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_mr_url.html)- mr_ - url
- Parse a merge request URL into its components.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_project_url.html)- project_ - url
- Parse a GitLab project URL into (base_url, project_path).
- [project_](https://docs.rs/fn.project_path_from_issue_url.html)- path_ - from_ - issue_ - url
- Extract the project path from a GitLab issue or work item web_url.
- [project_](https://docs.rs/fn.project_releases.html)- releases
- List releases for a project. Returns an empty list on 404 (project gone) so callers can iterate over many projects without per-project error handling.
- [project_](https://docs.rs/fn.project_summary.html)- summary
- Look up a project’s `path_with_namespace`from its numeric ID. Used to map event`project_id`→ group-prefix filter.
- [user_](https://docs.rs/fn.user_by_username.html)- by_ - username
- Look up a user by username on a specific GitLab instance.
Returns `Ok(None)`if the server returns 200 with an empty list (no user with that name on that instance).
- [user_](https://docs.rs/fn.user_events.html)- events
- Fetch a user’s activity events within `[after, before)`— GitLab’s event endpoint is half-open on both sides and rejects both-null. Results are paginated at 100/page; this follows every page until a short page arrives.
- [validate_](https://docs.rs/fn.validate_token.html)- token
- Check whether a token is valid by calling `GET /api/v4/user`.

# rodio 0.22.2 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rodio/0.22.2

# Audio playback library

Rust playback library.

Playback is handled by [cpal](https://github.com/RustAudio/cpal). Format decoding is handled by [Symphonia](https://github.com/pdeljanov/Symphonia) by default, or by optional format-specific decoders:

See [the feature flags](https://docs.rs/crate/rodio/latest/features) for more details on formats, and other features.

[The documentation](http://docs.rs/rodio) contains an introduction to the library.

We have written an upgrade [guide](https://docs.rs/UPGRADE.md). It will help you upgrade to rodio 0.21.

We are always making changes to rodio. This can mean that the examples do not work with the current crates.io release. You will have to look at the examples from commit `f7aa48d`. They are available [on github](https://github.com/RustAudio/rodio/tree/f7aa48daa08a303e247d68a1dad0dbcc915ca135/examples).

## Requirements

Rodio playback works in environments supported by [cpal](https://github.com/RustAudio/cpal) library.

The CPU of the target system should have hardware support for 32-bit floating point (`f32`), and atomic operations that are at least 32 bit wide. Without these the CPU may not be fast enough to keep up with real-time.

### Minimum Supported Rust Version (MSRV)

Rodio will keep a rolling MSRV (minimum supported rust version) policy of at least 6 months. When increasing the MSRV, the new Rust version must have been released at least six months ago.

## Dependencies (Linux only)

Rodio uses `cpal` library to send audio to the OS for playback. ALSA development files are needed to build `cpal` on Linux. These are provided as part of the `libasound2-dev` package on Debian and Ubuntu distributions and `alsa-lib-devel` on Fedora.

### Minimal build

It is possible to build `rodio` without support for audio playback. In this configuration `cpal` dependency and its requirements are excluded. This configuration may be useful, for example, for decoding and processing audio in environments when the audio output is not available (e.g. in case of Linux, when ALSA is not available). See `into_file` example that works with this build.

In order to use `rodio` in this configuration disable default features and add the necessary ones. In this case the `Cargo.toml` dependency would look like:

```
[]
 = {  = "0.22.1",  = false,  = ["symphonia-all"] }
```
### Cross compling aarch64/arm

Through cpal rodio depends on the alsa library (libasound & libasound-dev), this can make crosscompiling hard. Cpal has some guides on crosscompling in their Readme ([https://github.com/RustAudio/cpal](https://github.com/RustAudio/cpal)). They are missing instructions on aarch64 (arm linux) so we have some here:

#### aarch64/arm on Debian like (Ubuntu/pop)

- Install crossbuild-essential-arm64: `sudo apt-get install crossbuild-essential-arm64 clang`
- Add the aarch64 target for rust: `rustup target add aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu`
- Add the architecture arm64 to apt using: `sudo dpkg --add-architecture arm64`
- Install the [multi-arch](https://wiki.debian.org/Multiarch/HOWTO)version of libasound2-dev for arm64 using:`sudo apt install libasound2-dev:arm64`
- Build with the pkg config sysroot set to /usr/aarch64-linux-gnu and aarch64-linux-gnu as linker: `PKG_CONFIG_SYSROOT_DIR=/usr/aarch64-linux-gnu RUSTFLAGS="-C linker=aarch64-linux-gnu-gcc" cargo build --target aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu`

This will work for other Linux targets too if you change the architecture in the command and if there are multi-arch packages available.

You might want to look at [cross](https://github.com/cross-rs/cross) if you are running on a non debian system or want to make this more repeatable.

# Goals

- Simple API
- you should not need to know anything about audio to use rodio
- its hard to make mistakes
- easy to move rodio parts around your program

- Optimal
- rodio should be a zero cost abstraction
- rodio should offer options between perfect and fast

- extensible
- if something is missing in rodio it should be easy to add
- you should be able to control rodio parts easily

# Contributing

We love it when people join making rodio better. There are many ways to help not matter how experienced you are with audio or Rust. We would especially love help with:

- Reviewing PR's: we rely on the community to keep rodio correct, fast and maintainable. Absolutely anyone is welcome to leave reviews. Anyone can catch missing or unnecessary tests, unclear docs logic mistakes etc.
- Improving the docs: You only learn something for the first time once. Many of us forgot what was hard when things where new. Your experience using rodio for the first time can really help out here. You probably know best what needs clearification and how it should be written down. It can be anything, maybe a paragraph on audio theory or an extra example.
- Adding features: we love it when we get new features or existing onces get even better. Let us know what you are working on early. Not only can the rest of the community help out with the design we can help make the review and merge smooth. Please see our [Contributing Guide](https://docs.rs/CONTRIBUTING.md)for more to get you started.

                    rodio 0.22.2

# rodio - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rodio/0.22.2/target-redirect/rodio/

## Expand description

Audio playback library.

The main concept of this library is the [ Source](https://docs.rs/source/trait.Source.html) trait, which
represents a sound (streaming or not). In order to play a sound, there are three steps:

- Get an OS-Sink handle to a physical device. For example, get a sink to the system’s
default sound device with `DeviceSinkBuilder::open_default_sink()`
- Create an object that represents the streaming sound. It can be a sine wave, a buffer, a
`decoder``Source`
- Add the source to the OS-Sink using `MixerDeviceSink::mixer()`

Here is a complete example of how you would play an audio file:

```
use std::fs::File;
use rodio::{Decoder, MixerDeviceSink, source::Source};
// Get an OS-Sink handle to the default physical sound device.
// Note that the playback stops when the handle is dropped.//!
let handle = rodio::DeviceSinkBuilder::open_default_sink()
        .expect("open default audio stream");
let player = rodio::Player::connect_new(&handle.mixer());
// Load a sound from a file, using a path relative to Cargo.toml
let file = File::open("examples/music.ogg").unwrap();
// Decode that sound file into a source
let source = Decoder::try_from(file).unwrap();
// Play the sound directly on the device
handle.mixer().add(source);
// The sound plays in a separate audio thread,
// so we need to keep the main thread alive while it's playing.
std::thread::sleep(std::time::Duration::from_secs(5));
```
[ rodio::play()](https://docs.rs/stream/fn.play.html) helps to simplify the above

```
use std::fs::File;
use std::io::BufReader;
use rodio::{Decoder, MixerDeviceSink, source::Source};
// Get an OS-Sink handle to the default physical sound device.
// Note that the playback stops when the sink_handle is dropped.
let sink_handle = rodio::DeviceSinkBuilder::open_default_sink()
        .expect("open default audio stream");
// Load a sound from a file, using a path relative to Cargo.toml
let file = BufReader::new(File::open("examples/music.ogg").unwrap());
// Note that the playback stops when the player is dropped
let player = rodio::play(&sink_handle.mixer(), file).unwrap();
// The sound plays in a separate audio thread,
// so we need to keep the main thread alive while it's playing.
std::thread::sleep(std::time::Duration::from_secs(5));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#player)Player

In order to make it easier to control the playback, the rodio library also provides a type
named [ Player](https://docs.rs/struct.Player.html) which represents an audio track.

[plays its input sources sequentially, one after another. To play sounds in simultaneously in parallel, use](https://docs.rs/struct.Player.html)

`Player`[instead.](https://docs.rs/mixer/struct.Mixer.html)

`mixer::Mixer`To play a song Create a [ Player](https://docs.rs/struct.Player.html), connect it to the OS-Sink,
and

[your sound to it.](https://docs.rs/struct.Player.html#method.append)

`.append()````
use std::time::Duration;
use rodio::{MixerDeviceSink, Player};
use rodio::source::{SineWave, Source};
// _stream must live as long as the sink
let handle = rodio::DeviceSinkBuilder::open_default_sink()
        .expect("open default audio stream");
let player = rodio::Player::connect_new(&handle.mixer());
// Add a dummy source of the sake of the example.
let source = SineWave::new(440.0).take_duration(Duration::from_secs_f32(0.25)).amplify(0.20);
player.append(source);
// The sound plays in a separate thread. This call will block the current thread until the
// player has finished playing all its queued sounds.
player.sleep_until_end();
```
The [ append](https://docs.rs/struct.Player.html#method.append) method will add the sound at the end of the
player. It will be played when all the previous sounds have been played. If you want multiple
sounds to play simultaneously consider building your own

[from rodio parts.](https://docs.rs/struct.Player.html)

`Player`The [ Player](https://docs.rs/struct.Player.html) type also provides utilities such as playing/pausing or controlling the volume.

[§](https://docs.rs#filters)Filters

The [ Source](https://docs.rs/source/trait.Source.html) trait provides various filters, similar to the standard

[trait.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/iter/traits/iterator/trait.Iterator.html)

`Iterator`Example:

```
use rodio::Source;
use std::time::Duration;
// Repeats the first five seconds of the sound forever.
let source = source.take_duration(Duration::from_secs(5)).repeat_infinite();
```
[§](https://docs.rs#decoder-backends)Decoder Backends

[Symphonia](https://github.com/pdeljanov/Symphonia) is the default decoder library.
Rodio supports enabling all of Symphonia’s codecs using the `symphonia-all` feature
or enabling specific codecs using one of the `symphonia-{codec name}` features.
By default, decoders for the most common file types (flac, mp3, mp4, vorbis, wav) are enabled.

[§](https://docs.rs#alternative-decoders)Alternative Decoders

Alternative decoder libraries are available for some filetypes:

- claxon (flac)
- hound (wav)
- lewton (vorbis)
- minimp3 (mp3)

Symphonia is recommended for most usage. However, the alternative decoders are all licensed under either MIT or Apache 2.0 while Symphonia is licensed under MPL-2.0, so this may be a factor if you have strict licensing requirements.

If you enable one of these, you may want to set `default-features = false`
to avoid adding extra crates to your binary.
See the [available feature flags](https://docs.rs/crate/rodio/latest/features) for all options.

[§](https://docs.rs#optional-features)Optional Features

Rodio provides several optional features that are guarded with feature gates.

[§](https://docs.rs#feature-tracing)Feature “tracing”

The “tracing” feature replaces the print to stderr when a stream error happens with a recording an error event with tracing.

[§](https://docs.rs#feature-noise)Feature “noise”

The “noise” feature adds support for white and pink noise sources. This feature requires the “rand” crate.

[§](https://docs.rs#feature-playback)Feature “playback”

The “playback” feature adds support for playing audio. This feature requires the “cpal” crate.

[§](https://docs.rs#feature-64bit)Feature “64bit”

The “64bit” feature enables 64-bit sample precision using `f64` for audio samples and most
internal calculations. By default, rodio uses 32-bit floats (`f32`), which offers better
performance and is sufficient for most use cases. The 64-bit mode addresses precision drift
when chaining many audio operations together and in long-running signal generators where
phase errors compound over time.

[§](https://docs.rs#how-it-works-under-the-hood)How it works under the hood

Rodio spawns a background thread that is dedicated to reading from the sources and sending
the output to the device. Whenever you give up ownership of a [ Source](https://docs.rs/source/trait.Source.html) in order to play it,
it is sent to this background thread where it will be read by rodio.

All the sounds are mixed together by rodio before being sent to the operating system or the hardware. Therefore, there is no restriction on the number of sounds that play simultaneously or on the number of sinks that can be created (except for the fact that creating too many will slow down your program).

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [wav_](https://docs.rs/fn.wav_to_file.html)- to_ - file - `wav_output`
- Saves Source’s output into a wav file. The output samples format is 32-bit float. This function is intended primarily for testing and diagnostics. It can be used to see the output without opening OS-Sink to a real audio device.
- [wav_](https://docs.rs/fn.wav_to_writer.html)- to_ - writer - `wav_output`
- Saves Source’s output into a writer. The output samples format is 32-bit float. This function is intended primarily for testing and diagnostics. It can be used to see the output without opening an OS-Sink to a real audio device.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [BitDepth](https://docs.rs/type.BitDepth.html)
- Number of bits per sample. Can never be zero.
- [Channel](https://docs.rs/type.ChannelCount.html)- Count
- Number of channels in a stream. Can never be Zero
- [Float](https://docs.rs/type.Float.html)- `64bit`
- Floating point type used for internal calculations. Can be configured to be
either `f32`(default) or`f64`using the`64bit`feature flag.
- [Input](https://docs.rs/type.InputDevices.html)- Devices - `playback`
- A host’s device iterator yielding only *input*devices.
- [Output](https://docs.rs/type.OutputDevices.html)- Devices - `playback`
- A host’s device iterator yielding only *output*devices.
- [Sample](https://docs.rs/type.Sample.html)
- Represents value of a single sample.
Silence corresponds to the value `0.0`. The expected amplitude range is -1.0…1.0. Values below and above this range are clipped in conversion to other sample types. Use conversion traits from[dasp_sample](https://docs.rs/dasp_sample/0.11.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/dasp_sample/index.html)crate or[crate::conversions::SampleTypeConverter](https://docs.rs/conversions/struct.SampleTypeConverter.html)to convert between sample types if necessary.
- [Sample](https://docs.rs/type.SampleRate.html)- Rate
- Sample rate (a frame rate or samples per second per channel).

# rodio - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rodio/0.22.2/rodio/index.html

## Expand description

Audio playback library.

The main concept of this library is the [ Source](https://docs.rs/source/trait.Source.html) trait, which
represents a sound (streaming or not). In order to play a sound, there are three steps:

- Get an OS-Sink handle to a physical device. For example, get a sink to the system’s
default sound device with `DeviceSinkBuilder::open_default_sink()`
- Create an object that represents the streaming sound. It can be a sine wave, a buffer, a
`decoder``Source`
- Add the source to the OS-Sink using `MixerDeviceSink::mixer()`

Here is a complete example of how you would play an audio file:

```
use std::fs::File;
use rodio::{Decoder, MixerDeviceSink, source::Source};
// Get an OS-Sink handle to the default physical sound device.
// Note that the playback stops when the handle is dropped.//!
let handle = rodio::DeviceSinkBuilder::open_default_sink()
        .expect("open default audio stream");
let player = rodio::Player::connect_new(&handle.mixer());
// Load a sound from a file, using a path relative to Cargo.toml
let file = File::open("examples/music.ogg").unwrap();
// Decode that sound file into a source
let source = Decoder::try_from(file).unwrap();
// Play the sound directly on the device
handle.mixer().add(source);
// The sound plays in a separate audio thread,
// so we need to keep the main thread alive while it's playing.
std::thread::sleep(std::time::Duration::from_secs(5));
```
[ rodio::play()](https://docs.rs/stream/fn.play.html) helps to simplify the above

```
use std::fs::File;
use std::io::BufReader;
use rodio::{Decoder, MixerDeviceSink, source::Source};
// Get an OS-Sink handle to the default physical sound device.
// Note that the playback stops when the sink_handle is dropped.
let sink_handle = rodio::DeviceSinkBuilder::open_default_sink()
        .expect("open default audio stream");
// Load a sound from a file, using a path relative to Cargo.toml
let file = BufReader::new(File::open("examples/music.ogg").unwrap());
// Note that the playback stops when the player is dropped
let player = rodio::play(&sink_handle.mixer(), file).unwrap();
// The sound plays in a separate audio thread,
// so we need to keep the main thread alive while it's playing.
std::thread::sleep(std::time::Duration::from_secs(5));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#player)Player

In order to make it easier to control the playback, the rodio library also provides a type
named [ Player](https://docs.rs/struct.Player.html) which represents an audio track.

[plays its input sources sequentially, one after another. To play sounds in simultaneously in parallel, use](https://docs.rs/struct.Player.html)

`Player`[instead.](https://docs.rs/mixer/struct.Mixer.html)

`mixer::Mixer`To play a song Create a [ Player](https://docs.rs/struct.Player.html), connect it to the OS-Sink,
and

[your sound to it.](https://docs.rs/struct.Player.html#method.append)

`.append()````
use std::time::Duration;
use rodio::{MixerDeviceSink, Player};
use rodio::source::{SineWave, Source};
// _stream must live as long as the sink
let handle = rodio::DeviceSinkBuilder::open_default_sink()
        .expect("open default audio stream");
let player = rodio::Player::connect_new(&handle.mixer());
// Add a dummy source of the sake of the example.
let source = SineWave::new(440.0).take_duration(Duration::from_secs_f32(0.25)).amplify(0.20);
player.append(source);
// The sound plays in a separate thread. This call will block the current thread until the
// player has finished playing all its queued sounds.
player.sleep_until_end();
```
The [ append](https://docs.rs/struct.Player.html#method.append) method will add the sound at the end of the
player. It will be played when all the previous sounds have been played. If you want multiple
sounds to play simultaneously consider building your own

[from rodio parts.](https://docs.rs/struct.Player.html)

`Player`The [ Player](https://docs.rs/struct.Player.html) type also provides utilities such as playing/pausing or controlling the volume.

[§](https://docs.rs#filters)Filters

The [ Source](https://docs.rs/source/trait.Source.html) trait provides various filters, similar to the standard

[trait.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/iter/traits/iterator/trait.Iterator.html)

`Iterator`Example:

```
use rodio::Source;
use std::time::Duration;
// Repeats the first five seconds of the sound forever.
let source = source.take_duration(Duration::from_secs(5)).repeat_infinite();
```
[§](https://docs.rs#decoder-backends)Decoder Backends

[Symphonia](https://github.com/pdeljanov/Symphonia) is the default decoder library.
Rodio supports enabling all of Symphonia’s codecs using the `symphonia-all` feature
or enabling specific codecs using one of the `symphonia-{codec name}` features.
By default, decoders for the most common file types (flac, mp3, mp4, vorbis, wav) are enabled.

[§](https://docs.rs#alternative-decoders)Alternative Decoders

Alternative decoder libraries are available for some filetypes:

- claxon (flac)
- hound (wav)
- lewton (vorbis)
- minimp3 (mp3)

Symphonia is recommended for most usage. However, the alternative decoders are all licensed under either MIT or Apache 2.0 while Symphonia is licensed under MPL-2.0, so this may be a factor if you have strict licensing requirements.

If you enable one of these, you may want to set `default-features = false`
to avoid adding extra crates to your binary.
See the [available feature flags](https://docs.rs/crate/rodio/latest/features) for all options.

[§](https://docs.rs#optional-features)Optional Features

Rodio provides several optional features that are guarded with feature gates.

[§](https://docs.rs#feature-tracing)Feature “tracing”

The “tracing” feature replaces the print to stderr when a stream error happens with a recording an error event with tracing.

[§](https://docs.rs#feature-noise)Feature “noise”

The “noise” feature adds support for white and pink noise sources. This feature requires the “rand” crate.

[§](https://docs.rs#feature-playback)Feature “playback”

The “playback” feature adds support for playing audio. This feature requires the “cpal” crate.

[§](https://docs.rs#feature-64bit)Feature “64bit”

The “64bit” feature enables 64-bit sample precision using `f64` for audio samples and most
internal calculations. By default, rodio uses 32-bit floats (`f32`), which offers better
performance and is sufficient for most use cases. The 64-bit mode addresses precision drift
when chaining many audio operations together and in long-running signal generators where
phase errors compound over time.

[§](https://docs.rs#how-it-works-under-the-hood)How it works under the hood

Rodio spawns a background thread that is dedicated to reading from the sources and sending
the output to the device. Whenever you give up ownership of a [ Source](https://docs.rs/source/trait.Source.html) in order to play it,
it is sent to this background thread where it will be read by rodio.

All the sounds are mixed together by rodio before being sent to the operating system or the hardware. Therefore, there is no restriction on the number of sounds that play simultaneously or on the number of sinks that can be created (except for the fact that creating too many will slow down your program).

# lib.rs - source

Source: https://docs.rs/rodio/0.22.2/src/rodio/lib.rs.html

# rodio/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)//! Audio playback library.
[2](https://docs.rs#2)//!
[3](https://docs.rs#3)//! The main concept of this library is the [`Source`] trait, which
[4](https://docs.rs#4)//! represents a sound (streaming or not). In order to play a sound, there are three steps:
[5](https://docs.rs#5)//!
[6](https://docs.rs#6)//! - Get an OS-Sink handle to a physical device. For example, get a sink to the system's
[7](https://docs.rs#7)//!   default sound device with [`DeviceSinkBuilder::open_default_sink()`].
[8](https://docs.rs#8)//! - Create an object that represents the streaming sound. It can be a sine wave, a buffer, a
[9](https://docs.rs#9)//!   [`decoder`], etc. or even your own type that implements the [`Source`] trait.
[10](https://docs.rs#10)//! - Add the source to the OS-Sink using [`MixerDeviceSink::mixer()`]
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//!   on the OS-Sink handle.
[12](https://docs.rs#12)//!
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//! Here is a complete example of how you would play an audio file:
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//!
[15](https://docs.rs#15)#![cfg_attr(not(feature = "playback"), doc = "```ignore")]
[16](https://docs.rs#16)#![cfg_attr(feature = "playback", doc = "```no_run")]
[17](https://docs.rs#17)//! use std::fs::File;
[18](https://docs.rs#18)//! use rodio::{Decoder, MixerDeviceSink, source::Source};
[19](https://docs.rs#19)//!
[20](https://docs.rs#20)//! // Get an OS-Sink handle to the default physical sound device.
[21](https://docs.rs#21)//! // Note that the playback stops when the handle is dropped.//!
[22](https://docs.rs#22)//! let handle = rodio::DeviceSinkBuilder::open_default_sink()
[23](https://docs.rs#23)//!         .expect("open default audio stream");
[24](https://docs.rs#24)//! let player = rodio::Player::connect_new(&handle.mixer());
[25](https://docs.rs#25)//! // Load a sound from a file, using a path relative to Cargo.toml
[26](https://docs.rs#26)//! let file = File::open("examples/music.ogg").unwrap();
[27](https://docs.rs#27)//! // Decode that sound file into a source
[28](https://docs.rs#28)//! let source = Decoder::try_from(file).unwrap();
[29](https://docs.rs#29)//! // Play the sound directly on the device
[30](https://docs.rs#30)//! handle.mixer().add(source);
[31](https://docs.rs#31)//!
[32](https://docs.rs#32)//! // The sound plays in a separate audio thread,
[33](https://docs.rs#33)//! // so we need to keep the main thread alive while it's playing.
[34](https://docs.rs#34)//! std::thread::sleep(std::time::Duration::from_secs(5));
[35](https://docs.rs#35)//! ```
[36](https://docs.rs#36)//!
[37](https://docs.rs#37)//! [`rodio::play()`](crate::play) helps to simplify the above
[38](https://docs.rs#38)#![cfg_attr(not(feature = "playback"), doc = "```ignore")]
[39](https://docs.rs#39)#![cfg_attr(feature = "playback", doc = "```no_run")]
[40](https://docs.rs#40)//! use std::fs::File;
[41](https://docs.rs#41)//! use std::io::BufReader;
[42](https://docs.rs#42)//! use rodio::{Decoder, MixerDeviceSink, source::Source};
[43](https://docs.rs#43)//!
[44](https://docs.rs#44)//! // Get an OS-Sink handle to the default physical sound device.
[45](https://docs.rs#45)//! // Note that the playback stops when the sink_handle is dropped.
[46](https://docs.rs#46)//! let sink_handle = rodio::DeviceSinkBuilder::open_default_sink()
[47](https://docs.rs#47)//!         .expect("open default audio stream");
[48](https://docs.rs#48)//!
[49](https://docs.rs#49)//! // Load a sound from a file, using a path relative to Cargo.toml
[50](https://docs.rs#50)//! let file = BufReader::new(File::open("examples/music.ogg").unwrap());
[51](https://docs.rs#51)//! // Note that the playback stops when the player is dropped
[52](https://docs.rs#52)//! let player = rodio::play(&sink_handle.mixer(), file).unwrap();
[53](https://docs.rs#53)//!
[54](https://docs.rs#54)//! // The sound plays in a separate audio thread,
[55](https://docs.rs#55)//! // so we need to keep the main thread alive while it's playing.
[56](https://docs.rs#56)//! std::thread::sleep(std::time::Duration::from_secs(5));
[57](https://docs.rs#57)//! ```
[58](https://docs.rs#58)//!
[59](https://docs.rs#59)//!
[60](https://docs.rs#60)//! ## Player
[61](https://docs.rs#61)//!
[62](https://docs.rs#62)//! In order to make it easier to control the playback, the rodio library also provides a type
[63](https://docs.rs#63)//! named [`Player`] which represents an audio track. [`Player`] plays its input sources sequentially,
[64](https://docs.rs#64)//! one after another. To play sounds in simultaneously in parallel, use [`mixer::Mixer`] instead.
[65](https://docs.rs#65)//!
[66](https://docs.rs#66)//! To play a song Create a [`Player`], connect it to the OS-Sink,
[67](https://docs.rs#67)//! and [`.append()`](Player::append) your sound to it.
[68](https://docs.rs#68)//!
[69](https://docs.rs#69)#![cfg_attr(not(feature = "playback"), doc = "```ignore")]
[70](https://docs.rs#70)#![cfg_attr(feature = "playback", doc = "```no_run")]
[71](https://docs.rs#71)//! use std::time::Duration;
[72](https://docs.rs#72)//! use rodio::{MixerDeviceSink, Player};
[73](https://docs.rs#73)//! use rodio::source::{SineWave, Source};
[74](https://docs.rs#74)//!
[75](https://docs.rs#75)//! // _stream must live as long as the sink
[76](https://docs.rs#76)//! let handle = rodio::DeviceSinkBuilder::open_default_sink()
[77](https://docs.rs#77)//!         .expect("open default audio stream");
[78](https://docs.rs#78)//! let player = rodio::Player::connect_new(&handle.mixer());
[79](https://docs.rs#79)//!
[80](https://docs.rs#80)//! // Add a dummy source of the sake of the example.
[81](https://docs.rs#81)//! let source = SineWave::new(440.0).take_duration(Duration::from_secs_f32(0.25)).amplify(0.20);
[82](https://docs.rs#82)//! player.append(source);
[83](https://docs.rs#83)//!
[84](https://docs.rs#84)//! // The sound plays in a separate thread. This call will block the current thread until the
[85](https://docs.rs#85)//! // player has finished playing all its queued sounds.
[86](https://docs.rs#86)//! player.sleep_until_end();
[87](https://docs.rs#87)//! ```
[88](https://docs.rs#88)//!
[89](https://docs.rs#89)//! The [`append`](Player::append) method will add the sound at the end of the
[90](https://docs.rs#90)//! player. It will be played when all the previous sounds have been played. If you want multiple
[91](https://docs.rs#91)//! sounds to play simultaneously consider building your own [`Player`] from rodio parts.
[92](https://docs.rs#92)//!
[93](https://docs.rs#93)//! The [`Player`] type also provides utilities such as playing/pausing or controlling the volume.
[94](https://docs.rs#94)//!
[95](https://docs.rs#95)//! <div class="warning">Note that playback through Player will end if the associated
[96](https://docs.rs#96)//! DeviceSink is dropped.</div>
[97](https://docs.rs#97)//!
[98](https://docs.rs#98)//! ## Filters
[99](https://docs.rs#99)//!
[100](https://docs.rs#100)//! The [`Source`] trait provides various filters, similar to the standard [`Iterator`] trait.
[101](https://docs.rs#101)//!
[102](https://docs.rs#102)//! Example:
[103](https://docs.rs#103)//!
[104](https://docs.rs#104)#![cfg_attr(not(feature = "playback"), doc = "```ignore")]
[105](https://docs.rs#105)#![cfg_attr(feature = "playback", doc = "```")]
[106](https://docs.rs#106)//! use rodio::Source;
[107](https://docs.rs#107)//! use std::time::Duration;
[108](https://docs.rs#108)//!
[109](https://docs.rs#109)//! // Repeats the first five seconds of the sound forever.
[110](https://docs.rs#110)//! # let source = rodio::source::SineWave::new(440.0);
[111](https://docs.rs#111)//! let source = source.take_duration(Duration::from_secs(5)).repeat_infinite();
[112](https://docs.rs#112)//! ```
[113](https://docs.rs#113)//!
[114](https://docs.rs#114)//! ## Decoder Backends
[115](https://docs.rs#115)//!
[116](https://docs.rs#116)//! [Symphonia](https://github.com/pdeljanov/Symphonia) is the default decoder library.
[117](https://docs.rs#117)//! Rodio supports enabling all of Symphonia's codecs using the `symphonia-all` feature
[118](https://docs.rs#118)//! or enabling specific codecs using one of the `symphonia-{codec name}` features.
[119](https://docs.rs#119)//! By default, decoders for the most common file types (flac, mp3, mp4, vorbis, wav) are enabled.
[120](https://docs.rs#120)//!
[121](https://docs.rs#121)//! ### Alternative Decoders
[122](https://docs.rs#122)//!
[123](https://docs.rs#123)//! Alternative decoder libraries are available for some filetypes:
[124](https://docs.rs#124)//!
[125](https://docs.rs#125)//! - claxon (flac)
[126](https://docs.rs#126)//! - hound (wav)
[127](https://docs.rs#127)//! - lewton (vorbis)
[128](https://docs.rs#128)//! - minimp3 (mp3)
[129](https://docs.rs#129)//!
[130](https://docs.rs#130)//! Symphonia is recommended for most usage. However, the alternative decoders are all licensed
[131](https://docs.rs#131)//! under either MIT or Apache 2.0 while Symphonia is licensed under MPL-2.0, so
[132](https://docs.rs#132)//! this may be a factor if you have strict licensing requirements.
[133](https://docs.rs#133)//!
[134](https://docs.rs#134)//! If you enable one of these, you may want to set `default-features = false`
[135](https://docs.rs#135)//! to avoid adding extra crates to your binary.
[136](https://docs.rs#136)//! See the [available feature flags](https://docs.rs/crate/rodio/latest/features) for all options.
[137](https://docs.rs#137)//!
[138](https://docs.rs#138)//! ## Optional Features
[139](https://docs.rs#139)//!
[140](https://docs.rs#140)//! Rodio provides several optional features that are guarded with feature gates.
[141](https://docs.rs#141)//!
[142](https://docs.rs#142)//! ### Feature "tracing"
[143](https://docs.rs#143)//!
[144](https://docs.rs#144)//! The "tracing" feature replaces the print to stderr when a stream error happens with a
[145](https://docs.rs#145)//! recording an error event with tracing.
[146](https://docs.rs#146)//!
[147](https://docs.rs#147)//! ### Feature "noise"
[148](https://docs.rs#148)//!
[149](https://docs.rs#149)//! The "noise" feature adds support for white and pink noise sources. This feature requires the
[150](https://docs.rs#150)//! "rand" crate.
[151](https://docs.rs#151)//!
[152](https://docs.rs#152)//! ### Feature "playback"
[153](https://docs.rs#153)//!
[154](https://docs.rs#154)//! The "playback" feature adds support for playing audio. This feature requires the "cpal" crate.
[155](https://docs.rs#155)//!
[156](https://docs.rs#156)//! ### Feature "64bit"
[157](https://docs.rs#157)//!
[158](https://docs.rs#158)//! The "64bit" feature enables 64-bit sample precision using `f64` for audio samples and most
[159](https://docs.rs#159)//! internal calculations. By default, rodio uses 32-bit floats (`f32`), which offers better
[160](https://docs.rs#160)//! performance and is sufficient for most use cases. The 64-bit mode addresses precision drift
[161](https://docs.rs#161)//! when chaining many audio operations together and in long-running signal generators where
[162](https://docs.rs#162)//! phase errors compound over time.
[163](https://docs.rs#163)//!
[164](https://docs.rs#164)//! ## How it works under the hood
[165](https://docs.rs#165)//!
[166](https://docs.rs#166)//! Rodio spawns a background thread that is dedicated to reading from the sources and sending
[167](https://docs.rs#167)//! the output to the device. Whenever you give up ownership of a [`Source`] in order to play it,
[168](https://docs.rs#168)//! it is sent to this background thread where it will be read by rodio.
[169](https://docs.rs#169)//!
[170](https://docs.rs#170)//! All the sounds are mixed together by rodio before being sent to the operating system or the
[171](https://docs.rs#171)//! hardware. Therefore, there is no restriction on the number of sounds that play simultaneously or
[172](https://docs.rs#172)//! on the number of sinks that can be created (except for the fact that creating too many will slow
[173](https://docs.rs#173)//! down your program).
[174](https://docs.rs#174)
[175](https://docs.rs#175)#![cfg_attr(
[176](https://docs.rs#176)    any(test, not(feature = "playback")),

[180](https://docs.rs#180)    allow(unused_variables),
[181](https://docs.rs#181)    allow(unreachable_code)
[182](https://docs.rs#182))]
[183](https://docs.rs#183)#![cfg_attr(docsrs, feature(doc_cfg))]

}## Expand description

A source of samples.

[§](https://docs.rs#a-quick-lesson-about-sounds)A quick lesson about sounds

[§](https://docs.rs#sampling)Sampling

A sound is a vibration that propagates through air and reaches your ears. This vibration can be represented as an analog signal.

In order to store this signal in the computer’s memory or on the disk, we perform what is
called *sampling*. This consists in choosing an interval of time (for example 20µs) and reading
the amplitude of the signal at each interval (for example, if the interval is 20µs we read the
amplitude every 20µs). By doing so we obtain a list of numerical values, each value being
called a *sample*.

Therefore, a sound can be represented in memory by a frequency and a list of samples. The frequency is expressed in hertz and corresponds to the number of samples that have been read per second. For example if we read one sample every 20µs, the frequency would be 50000 Hz. In reality, common values for the frequency are 44100, 48000 and 96000.

[§](https://docs.rs#channels)Channels

But a frequency and a list of values only represent one signal. When you listen to a sound,
your left and right ears don’t receive exactly the same signal. In order to handle this,
we usually record not one but two different signals: one for the left ear and one for the right
ear. We say that such a sound has two *channels*.

Sometimes sounds even have five or six channels, each corresponding to a location around the head of the listener.

The standard in audio manipulation is to *interleave* the multiple channels. In other words,
in a sound with two channels the list of samples contains the first sample of the first
channel, then the first sample of the second channel, then the second sample of the first
channel, then the second sample of the second channel, and so on. The same applies if you have
more than two channels. The rodio library only supports this schema.

Therefore, in order to represent a sound in memory in fact we need three characteristics: the frequency, the number of channels, and the list of samples.

[§](https://docs.rs#the-source-trait)The `Source` trait

A Rust object that represents a sound should implement the `Source` trait.

The three characteristics that describe a sound are provided through this trait:

- The number of channels can be retrieved with `channels`.
- The frequency can be retrieved with `sample_rate`.
- The list of values can be retrieved by iterating on the source. The `Source`trait requires that the`Iterator`trait be implemented as well. When a`Source`returns None the sound has ended.

[§](https://docs.rs#spans)Spans

The samples rate and number of channels of some sound sources can change by itself from time to time.

Note: As a basic example, if you play two audio files one after the other and treat the whole as a single source, then the channels and samples rate of that source may change at the transition between the two files.

However, for optimization purposes rodio supposes that the number of channels and the frequency
stay the same for long periods of time and avoids calling `channels()` and
`sample_rate` too frequently.

In order to properly handle this situation, the `current_span_len()` method should return
the number of samples that remain in the iterator before the samples rate and number of
channels can potentially change.

## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rodio/source/mod.rs.html#183)#### fn [current_span_len](https://docs.rs#tymethod.current_span_len)(&self) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rodio/source/mod.rs.html#183)

#### fn [current_span_len](https://docs.rs#tymethod.current_span_len)(&self) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)>

Returns the number of samples before the current span ends.

`None` means “infinite” or “until the sound ends”. Sources that return `Some(x)` should
return `Some(0)` if and only if when there’s no more data.

After the engine has finished reading the specified number of samples, it will check
whether the value of `channels()` and/or `sample_rate()` have changed.

[§](https://docs.rs#frame-alignment)Frame Alignment

Span lengths must be multiples of the channel count to ensure spans end on frame
boundaries. A “frame” is one sample for each channel. Returning a span length
that is not a multiple of `channels()` will cause channel misalignment issues.

Note: This returns the total span size, not the remaining samples. Use `Iterator::size_hint`
to determine how many samples remain in the iterator.
